0.title: Avoid SELECT * in large table queries
0.problem_description: Using SELECT * retrieves all columns from a table regardless of downstream need, causing unnecessary I/O, increased memory consumption, and preventing columnar storage optimizations such as column pruning.
0.root_cause: Developer convenience during prototyping; lack of schema awareness at query-writing time; absence of a query review or linting process.
0.optimization_strategy: Replace SELECT * with an explicit list of only the columns required by the downstream consumer or transformation step.
0.after_example: SELECT order_id, customer_id, status, created_at FROM orders WHERE status = 'active';
0.explanation: Columnar storage engines such as Spark, BigQuery, and Hive ORC read only the columns explicitly requested. Specifying columns enables column pruning at the storage layer, reduces bytes scanned, lowers executor memory pressure, and decreases shuffle costs in distributed environments. In wide tables with 50+ columns, this can eliminate 80–90% of I/O.

expected_impact.execution_time: 10–40% reduction depending on table width and storage format
expected_impact.cost: Medium reduction in cloud scan costs (BigQuery, Redshift)
expected_impact.memory: Proportional reduction based on number of columns eliminated

applicability_conditions: Wide tables with 20 or more columns
Columnar storage formats such as Parquet or ORC
OLAP and analytical workloads
Spark, BigQuery, Hive, Trino environments
0.source: AWS Data Engineering Best Practices Guide
0.embedding_text: Avoid SELECT * in large table queries. SELECT * retrieves all columns causing unnecessary I/O and memory usage. Replace SELECT * with explicit column list. SELECT * column pruning I/O optimization query rewrite columnar storage wide table.
0.notes: Less impactful on narrow tables with fewer than 5 columns, or on row-store engines for small point-lookup queries.

1.title: Use broadcast join for small lookup table joins
1.problem_description: Joining a large fact table with a small lookup or dimension table using a default shuffle join causes unnecessary cross-network data movement, increasing execution time and resource consumption.
1.root_cause: Default query planner treats all joins as shuffle joins unless explicitly hinted or auto-broadcast thresholds are configured. Small table size is not always detected automatically.
1.optimization_strategy: Use a broadcast join hint to replicate the small table to all executors, eliminating the shuffle phase entirely.
1.before_example: SELECT f.order_id, d.region_name FROM fact_orders f JOIN dim_region d ON f.region_id = d.region_id;
1.after_example: SELECT /*+ BROADCAST(d) */ f.order_id, d.region_name FROM fact_orders f JOIN dim_region d ON f.region_id = d.region_id;
1.explanation: In a shuffle join, both tables are repartitioned across all nodes by the join key, generating large network I/O. When one table is small enough to fit in executor memory (typically under 10MB–200MB depending on configuration), broadcasting it to every executor eliminates the shuffle entirely. This is one of the highest-impact single query optimizations in Spark workloads.

expected_impact.cost: High reduction — eliminates shuffle stage network I/O
expected_impact.memory: Small increase in executor memory for broadcast table; net positive

applicability_conditions: One side of the join is a small lookup or dimension table
Small table fits within executor memory limits
Distributed execution environment such as Spark or Hive
Join keys are present and selective
1.embedding_text: Use broadcast join for small lookup table joins. Default shuffle join on small dimension tables causes unnecessary network I/O. Use broadcast join hint to replicate small table to all executors. Broadcast join shuffle join join optimization Spark hint dimension table fact table network I/O.
1.notes: Broadcast threshold in Spark is controlled by spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold (default 10MB). Increase with caution — too large a broadcast table causes OOM errors.

2.title: Apply predicate pushdown to filter data early in execution
2.problem_description: Filters applied after joins or aggregations process more rows than necessary, increasing memory usage, shuffle size, and overall query execution time.
2.root_cause: Query written in logical order without considering physical execution plan; filters placed after joins in the SQL structure even when they could be applied earlier.
2.optimization_strategy: Rewrite queries to apply WHERE filters as early as possible — before joins, subqueries, or aggregations — so that fewer rows flow into expensive operations.
2.before_example: SELECT a.customer_id, SUM(b.amount) FROM customers a JOIN transactions b ON a.customer_id = b.customer_id GROUP BY a.customer_id HAVING a.country = 'IN';
2.after_example: SELECT a.customer_id, SUM(b.amount) FROM customers a JOIN transactions b ON a.customer_id = b.customer_id WHERE a.country = 'IN' GROUP BY a.customer_id;
2.explanation: Moving the filter on country from HAVING to WHERE allows the query optimizer to apply it before the join, significantly reducing the number of rows that enter the join and aggregation stages. Most modern optimizers (Spark Catalyst, PostgreSQL planner) will push predicates automatically, but explicitly placing filters early makes the intent clear and guarantees correct behavior in cases where the optimizer cannot infer pushdown safely.

expected_impact.cost: Medium to high — fewer rows shuffled across join and aggregation stages
expected_impact.memory: Proportional reduction in intermediate dataset size

applicability_conditions: Filter condition is on a column available before the join or aggregation
Filter has high selectivity — removes a significant fraction of rows
Query involves multi-table joins or GROUP BY operations
Optimizer may not automatically detect safe pushdown
2.source: Google BigQuery SQL Best Practices Documentation
2.embedding_text: Apply predicate pushdown to filter data early in execution. Filters after joins process more rows than necessary increasing memory and shuffle size. Apply WHERE filters before joins and aggregations. Predicate pushdown filter early WHERE clause HAVING clause join optimization query rewrite execution plan.
2.notes: Verify the filter is semantically equivalent when moved — HAVING filters on aggregated values cannot always be moved to WHERE.

3.title: Replace correlated subquery with JOIN or CTE
3.problem_description: Correlated subqueries execute once for every row in the outer query, causing O(n) repeated scans of the inner table and severely degrading performance at scale.
3.root_cause: Correlated subqueries are intuitive to write for row-by-row logic but are not optimized by most query planners. Developers often use them without understanding the execution cost.
3.optimization_strategy: Rewrite correlated subqueries as JOIN operations or Common Table Expressions (CTEs) that execute once and are joined back to the outer query.
3.before_example: SELECT order_id, amount FROM orders o WHERE amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders WHERE customer_id = o.customer_id);
3.after_example: WITH customer_avg AS (SELECT customer_id, AVG(amount) AS avg_amount FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) SELECT o.order_id, o.amount FROM orders o JOIN customer_avg ca ON o.customer_id = ca.customer_id WHERE o.amount > ca.avg_amount;
3.explanation: The correlated subquery computes AVG(amount) for every single row in the outer query — if orders has 10 million rows, the subquery runs 10 million times. The CTE-based rewrite computes the average once per customer_id group and joins the result back, reducing the operation from O(n) repeated scans to a single aggregation pass plus one join.

expected_impact.execution_time: 50–95% reduction for large tables — scales linearly with row count
expected_impact.cost: Very high — eliminates repeated full or partial table scans
expected_impact.memory: Moderate increase for CTE materialization; net strongly positive

applicability_conditions: Correlated subquery references an outer query column in its WHERE or HAVING clause
Inner table is large and scanned repeatedly
Aggregation in subquery is computable independently of each outer row
Query planner does not automatically decorrelate
3.source: SQL Query Optimization in Relational Database Systems — Das, 2020
3.embedding_text: Replace correlated subquery with JOIN or CTE. Correlated subqueries execute once per row causing repeated table scans. Rewrite as JOIN or CTE that executes once. Correlated subquery CTE common table expression join rewrite subquery optimization O(n) scan query rewrite.
3.notes: Some modern optimizers (BigQuery, PostgreSQL 12+) can decorrelate simple subqueries automatically. Verify execution plan before and after to confirm improvement.

4.title: Eliminate redundant transformation steps in ETL pipelines
4.problem_description: ETL pipelines often contain duplicate filter conditions, repeated column derivations, or the same transformation applied at multiple stages, increasing processing time, resource cost, and maintenance complexity.
4.root_cause: Pipelines built incrementally by multiple team members over time; lack of transformation audit or lineage review; copy-paste pattern reuse without consolidation.
4.optimization_strategy: Audit the transformation DAG to identify steps producing identical or derivable outputs. Consolidate duplicate filters and column derivations into a single upstream step and reuse the result downstream.
4.before_example:
# Step 1: Filter active records
df1 = df.filter(col('status') == 'active')
# Step 3 (later in pipeline): Filter active records again
df3 = df2.filter(col('status') == 'active')
4.after_example:
# Filter once and reuse
df_active = df.filter(col('status') == 'active')
# All downstream steps use df_active directly
4.explanation: Each redundant filter or transformation step in a Spark or PySpark pipeline forces a re-evaluation of the predicate or column derivation against the full dataset at that stage. Eliminating duplicates reduces the number of physical plan operations, lowers executor CPU usage, and reduces intermediate shuffle writes. In large pipelines, removing even two or three redundant steps can meaningfully reduce end-to-end execution time.

expected_impact.execution_time: 10–30% reduction depending on pipeline size and number of redundant steps
expected_impact.cost: Low to medium — reduces executor compute time

applicability_conditions: Pipeline has multiple transformation stages on the same dataset
Same filter condition appears more than once across stages
Column derivation is repeated rather than inherited from upstream
Pipeline was built incrementally or by multiple contributors
4.source: ETL Workflow Optimization Techniques in Data Engineering Systems — Kumar and Patel, IEEE Access 2021
4.embedding_text: Eliminate redundant transformation steps in ETL pipelines. Duplicate filters and column derivations increase processing time and cost. Consolidate duplicate steps into a single upstream transformation and reuse downstream. Redundant transformation ETL optimization pipeline audit DAG optimization PySpark filter deduplication transformation consolidation.
4.notes: Use Spark's explain() or DAG visualization in Airflow to identify redundant steps before manual code review.

5.title: Replace full reload with incremental delta processing
5.problem_description: Full table reloads on every pipeline run reprocess all historical data regardless of what has changed, causing unnecessary compute cost, longer execution times, and increased risk of downstream data freshness delays.
5.root_cause: Simplest implementation pattern during initial development; lack of change detection or watermark logic; schema does not include reliable updated_at or event_time columns.
5.optimization_strategy: Implement incremental processing using a high-watermark pattern — track the last successfully processed timestamp or ID, and on each run process only records newer than the watermark.
5.before_example:
# Full reload every run
df = spark.read.table('source_table')
df.write.mode('overwrite').saveAsTable('target_table')
5.after_example:
# Incremental load using watermark
last_watermark = get_last_watermark()  # e.g., '2026-05-14 00:00:00'
df = spark.read.table('source_table').filter(col('updated_at') > last_watermark)
df.write.mode('append').saveAsTable('target_table')
update_watermark(df.agg(max('updated_at')).collect()[0][0])
5.explanation: Full reloads scale linearly with data volume — doubling the table size doubles compute time and cost regardless of how little data changed. Incremental processing scales with the change volume, which in most production pipelines is a small fraction of total data. This pattern is essential for maintaining SLA compliance as datasets grow over time.

expected_impact.execution_time: 60–95% reduction for mature datasets with low daily change rates
expected_impact.cost: Very high — compute scales with change volume rather than total data volume
expected_impact.memory: Proportional to incremental batch size rather than full table

applicability_conditions: Source table has a reliable updated_at or event_time timestamp column
Target table supports append or upsert operations
Daily change volume is small relative to total historical data
Pipeline runs on a regular schedule (daily, hourly)
5.source: Databricks Delta Lake Documentation — Incremental Data Processing Patterns
5.embedding_text: Replace full reload with incremental delta processing. Full table reloads reprocess all historical data causing unnecessary compute cost. Use watermark pattern to process only new or changed records. Incremental processing delta load watermark full reload ETL optimization change data capture append mode.
5.notes: Requires source schema to have a monotonically increasing column (timestamp or ID). Late-arriving data must be handled separately with a lookback window.

6.title: Detect missing indexes on high-frequency filter columns
6.problem_description: Queries that repeatedly filter or join on columns without indexes perform full table scans on every execution, causing high I/O and long response times that scale poorly with data volume.
6.root_cause: Indexes not created during initial schema design; columns added later without index review; DBA oversight gaps in growing schemas.
6.optimization_strategy: Analyze query patterns to identify columns most frequently used in WHERE, JOIN ON, and ORDER BY clauses. Create targeted indexes on high-frequency, high-selectivity columns.
6.before_example:
-- No index on customer_id
SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE customer_id = 'C12345';  -- Full table scan
6.explanation: Without an index, the database engine reads every row in the table to find matching records — a cost that grows linearly with table size. An index on customer_id creates a sorted auxiliary structure that allows the engine to locate matching rows in O(log n) time. For high-cardinality columns used in frequent filter predicates, index creation is typically the single highest-impact schema change available.

expected_impact.execution_time: 70–99% reduction for point lookups and range scans on indexed columns
expected_impact.cost: Minimal index maintenance overhead on writes; major gain on reads
expected_impact.memory: Index storage adds 10–30% of column data size

applicability_conditions: Column is used frequently in WHERE or JOIN ON clauses
Column has high cardinality (many distinct values)
Workload is read-heavy relative to write-heavy
Table size is large enough that full scans are costly
6.source: PostgreSQL Documentation — Index Types and Usage
6.embedding_text: Detect missing indexes on high-frequency filter columns. Queries filtering on unindexed columns perform full table scans at high I/O cost. Create indexes on high-frequency high-selectivity WHERE and JOIN columns. Missing index index creation full table scan query performance WHERE clause JOIN optimization cardinality.
6.notes: Indexes slow down INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations. Avoid indexing on write-heavy tables unless read performance is critical. Composite indexes should match the column order in frequent query predicates.

7.title: Ensure queries use partition pruning to avoid full table scans
7.problem_description: Queries on partitioned tables that do not filter on the partition key scan all partitions, negating the performance and cost benefits of partitioning entirely.
7.root_cause: Query written without knowledge of table partition structure; partition column wrapped in a function or cast that prevents pruning; partition column not included in WHERE clause.
7.optimization_strategy: Ensure all queries on partitioned tables include a filter on the partition key in the WHERE clause, and avoid applying functions or type casts to the partition column that prevent partition elimination.
7.before_example:
-- Partitioned by event_date but filter uses a function on the column
SELECT user_id, event_type FROM events WHERE YEAR(event_date) = 2025;  -- Scans all partitions
7.after_example:
-- Filter directly on partition key range
SELECT user_id, event_type FROM events WHERE event_date BETWEEN '2025-01-01' AND '2025-12-31';  -- Prunes to 2025 partitions only
7.explanation: Partition pruning is the mechanism by which the query engine skips reading partitions that cannot contain rows matching the filter. When a function such as YEAR() is applied to the partition column, the optimizer cannot determine which partitions match without scanning all of them, defeating the purpose of partitioning. Using a direct range filter on the partition key allows the engine to identify and read only the relevant partitions, reducing I/O proportional to the fraction of data filtered.

expected_impact.execution_time: 50–90% reduction depending on fraction of partitions accessed
expected_impact.cost: Proportional reduction in bytes scanned — directly maps to cloud query cost savings
expected_impact.memory: Significant reduction in executor memory for scan stages

applicability_conditions: Table is partitioned by a date, region, or category column
Query filters on a column that matches the partition key
Partition column is not wrapped in a function or implicit cast
Table has a large number of partitions
7.source: Google BigQuery Partitioned Table Best Practices
7.embedding_text: Ensure queries use partition pruning to avoid full table scans. Queries not filtering on partition key scan all partitions negating partitioning benefits. Filter directly on partition key without functions to enable partition elimination. Partition pruning partition elimination full table scan partitioned table date partition query rewrite scan reduction.
7.notes: BigQuery requires the partition column to be filtered directly in the WHERE clause for pruning to work. Wrapping in DATE() or CAST() prevents pruning even in BigQuery.

8.title: Cache small lookup tables as Spark broadcast variables
8.problem_description: Small reference or lookup tables joined repeatedly across multiple Spark operations are re-read and re-shuffled on every use, generating unnecessary I/O and network overhead across the cluster.
8.root_cause: Lookup tables treated the same as large fact tables in the execution plan; broadcast threshold not configured or table size slightly exceeds auto-broadcast limit.
8.optimization_strategy: Explicitly cache small lookup DataFrames using Spark's broadcast() function or persist() with MEMORY_ONLY storage level so they are distributed once and reused from executor memory across all operations.
8.before_example:
# Lookup table re-read and shuffled on every join
for date in date_list:
    df = spark.read.table('fact_events').filter(col('event_date') == date)
    result = df.join(spark.read.table('dim_product'), 'product_id')  # Re-reads dim_product each time
    result.write.mode('append').saveAsTable('output')
8.after_example:
# Broadcast lookup table once before the loop
from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast
dim_product = broadcast(spark.read.table('dim_product'))  # Cached and distributed once
for date in date_list:
    df = spark.read.table('fact_events').filter(col('event_date') == date)
    result = df.join(dim_product, 'product_id')  # Uses cached broadcast copy
    result.write.mode('append').saveAsTable('output')
8.explanation: In the unoptimized version, dim_product is read from storage and shuffled to executors on every loop iteration. With broadcast caching, the table is serialized and sent to every executor once at the start and held in memory for the duration of the job. Subsequent joins use the in-memory copy without any additional I/O or network transfer. This is especially effective in iterative ETL pipelines that join the same small table repeatedly.

expected_impact.execution_time: 20–60% reduction in iterative pipelines joining the same small table multiple times
expected_impact.cost: High reduction in network I/O and storage read costs
expected_impact.memory: Small increase in executor memory; lookup table size is the upper bound

applicability_conditions: Lookup or dimension table is small enough to fit in executor memory
Same lookup table is joined more than once in a pipeline run
Pipeline runs iteratively over date ranges or batch partitions
Spark or PySpark execution environment
8.source: Apache Spark Documentation — Broadcast Variables and Shared Variables
8.embedding_text: Cache small lookup tables as Spark broadcast variables. Small lookup tables re-read and shuffled on every join causing unnecessary I/O. Use broadcast() to distribute small tables once and reuse from executor memory. Broadcast variable caching lookup table dimension table shuffle reduction Spark optimization memory caching iterative pipeline.
8.notes: Default Spark broadcast threshold is 10MB (spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold). For tables between 10MB–200MB, consider raising the threshold or using explicit broadcast() calls. Avoid broadcasting tables that change frequently across pipeline runs.

9.title: Detect pipeline bottlenecks from execution log task duration analysis
9.problem_description: Long-running pipelines often have one or two tasks that dominate total execution time, but without systematic log analysis these bottlenecks go undetected and optimization effort is spent on non-critical steps.
9.root_cause: No structured log analysis process; pipeline execution monitored by total runtime only rather than per-task breakdown; absence of alerting on task-level duration thresholds.
9.optimization_strategy: Parse pipeline execution logs to extract per-task start and end timestamps. Calculate task duration, identify tasks exceeding a configurable threshold, and flag the top-N slowest tasks for investigation.
9.before_example:
# No per-task analysis — only total pipeline duration monitored
[2026-05-14 02:00:00] Pipeline started
[2026-05-14 04:47:32] Pipeline completed — Total: 2h 47m
9.after_example:
# Per-task duration extracted from logs
Task: ingest_raw_events        Duration: 4m 12s   Status: OK
Task: join_customer_dimension  Duration: 1h 58m   Status: SLOW  <-- Bottleneck flagged
Task: aggregate_daily_metrics  Duration: 18m 43s  Status: OK
Task: write_output_table       Duration: 26m 11s  Status: OK
# Recommendation: Investigate join_customer_dimension — likely data skew or missing broadcast
9.explanation: The Pareto principle applies strongly to pipeline execution: a small number of tasks typically account for most of the runtime. By parsing execution logs to extract per-task durations, the system can identify which specific task is responsible for the bottleneck and direct optimization effort precisely. In the example, the join task accounts for over 70% of total pipeline time — a strong signal for data skew or join type investigation.

expected_impact.execution_time: Indirectly enables 30–70% reduction by correctly targeting optimization effort
expected_impact.cost: Reduces wasted engineering time spent optimizing non-bottleneck tasks
expected_impact.memory: No direct memory impact — analysis is diagnostic

applicability_conditions: Pipeline execution logs are available with per-task timestamps
Pipeline has multiple distinct tasks or stages
Total pipeline duration is significantly longer than expected
No existing per-task monitoring or alerting is in place
9.source: Apache Airflow Documentation — Task Monitoring and Log Management
9.embedding_text: Detect pipeline bottlenecks from execution log task duration analysis. Long-running pipelines have one or two tasks dominating execution time that go undetected without log analysis. Parse execution logs to extract per-task durations and flag slowest tasks. Bottleneck detection execution log analysis task duration pipeline monitoring Airflow slow task log parsing performance profiling.
9.notes: For Airflow pipelines, task duration is available from the task_instance table in the metadata database. For Spark, Stage and Task durations are in the Spark UI event logs and can be parsed programmatically using the Spark History Server REST API.

Introduction to optimizing query performance

This document provides an overview of optimization techniques that can improve
query performance in BigQuery. In general, queries that do less work
perform better. They run faster and consume fewer resources, which can result in
lower costs and fewer failures.

Query performance

Evaluating query performance in BigQuery involves several factors:

Input data and data sources (I/O)
:
How many bytes does your query read?

Communication between nodes (shuffling)
:
How many bytes does your query pass to the next stage? How many bytes does your
query pass to each slot?

Computation
:
How much CPU work does your query require?

Outputs (materialization)
:
How many bytes does your query write?

Capacity and concurrency
:
How many slots are available and how many other queries are running at the same time?

Query patterns
:
Are your queries following SQL best practices?

To evaluate specific queries or whether you are experiencing resource contention,
you can use
Cloud Monitoring
or the
BigQuery administrative resource charts
to monitor how your BigQuery jobs consume
resources over time. You can also use Gemini Cloud Assist to

analyze your jobs
.
If you identify a slow or resource-intensive query, you can
focus your performance optimizations on that query.

Some query patterns, especially those generated by business intelligence tools,
can be accelerated by using
BigQuery BI Engine
.
BI Engine is a fast, in-memory analysis service that accelerates many
SQL queries in BigQuery by intelligently caching the data you use
most frequently. BI Engine is built into BigQuery,
which means you can often get better performance without any query modifications.

As with any systems, optimizing for performance sometimes involves tradeoffs.
For example, using advanced SQL syntax can sometimes introduce complexity and
reduce the queries' understandability for people who aren't SQL experts.
Spending time on micro-optimizations for noncritical workloads could also divert
resources away from building new features for your applications or from identifying
more important optimizations. To help you achieve the highest possible return on
investment, we recommend that you focus your optimizations on the workloads that
matter most to your data analytics pipelines.

Optimization for capacity and concurrency

BigQuery offers two pricing models for queries:

on-demand
pricing and

capacity-based

pricing. The on-demand model provides a shared pool of capacity, and pricing is
based on the amount of data that is processed by each query you run.

The
capacity-based
model is
recommended if you want to budget a consistent, monthly expenditure
or if you need more capacity than is available with the on-demand model.
When you use capacity-based pricing, you allocate dedicated query processing
capacity that is measured in
slots
.
The cost of all bytes processed is included in the capacity-based price.
In addition to fixed
slot commitments
,
you can use
autoscaling slots
,
which provide dynamic capacity based on your query workload.

The performance of queries that are run repeatedly on the same data can vary,
and the variation is generally larger for queries using on-demand slots than
it is for queries using slot reservations.

During SQL query processing, BigQuery breaks down the
computational capacity required to execute each stage of a query into
slots. BigQuery automatically determines the
number of queries that can run concurrently as follows:

On-demand model: number of slots available in the project

Capacity-based model: number of slots available in the reservation

Queries that require more slots than are available are
queued

until processing resources become available. After a query begins execution,
BigQuery calculates how many slots each query stage
uses based on the stage size and complexity and the number of slots
available. BigQuery uses a technique called
fair scheduling

to ensure that each query has enough capacity to progress.

implies that you should never produce incomplete results from your tasks. An

duplicate rows in your database. Replace it with UPSERT.

data_interval_start

follow this partitioning method while writing data in S3/HDFS as well.

computation, as it leads to different outcomes on each run. It’s fine to use

25.text:
Normally, when any task fails, all other tasks are not executed and the whole Dag Run gets failed status too. But
when we use trigger rules, we can disrupt the normal flow of running tasks and the whole Dag may represent different
status that we expect. For example, we can have a teardown task (with trigger rule set to
TriggerRule.ALL_DONE
)
that will be executed regardless of the state of the other tasks (e.g. to clean up the resources). In such
situation, the Dag would always run this task and the Dag Run will get the status of this particular task, so we can
potentially lose the information about failing tasks. If we want to ensure that the Dag with teardown task would fail
if any task fails, we need to use the watcher pattern. The watcher task is a task that will always fail if
triggered, but it needs to be triggered only if any other task fails. It needs to have a trigger rule set to

TriggerRule.ONE_FAILED
and it needs also to be a downstream task for all other tasks in the Dag. Thanks to
this, if every other task will pass, the watcher will be skipped, but when something fails, the watcher task will be
executed and fail making the Dag Run fail too.

Note

Be aware that trigger rules only rely on the direct upstream (parent) tasks, e.g.
TriggerRule.ONE_FAILED

will ignore any failed (or
upstream_failed
) tasks that are not a direct parent of the parameterized task.

There are no “metrics” for Dag complexity, especially, there are no metrics that can tell you
whether your Dag is “simple enough”. However, as with any Python code, you can definitely tell that
your Dag code is “simpler” or “faster” when it is optimized. If you
want to optimize your Dags there are the following actions you can take:

Make your Dag load faster. This is a single improvement advice that might be implemented in various ways
but this is the one that has biggest impact on scheduler’s performance. Whenever you have a chance to make
your Dag load faster - go for it, if your goal is to improve performance. Look at the

Top level Python Code
to get some tips of how you can do it. Also see at

Dag Loader Test
on how to asses your Dag loading time.

Make your Dag generate simpler structure. Every task dependency adds additional processing overhead for
scheduling and execution. The Dag that has simple linear structure
A

->

B

->

C
will experience
less delays in task scheduling than Dag that has a deeply nested tree structure with exponentially growing
number of depending tasks for example. If you can make your Dags more linear - where at single point in
execution there are as few potential candidates to run among the tasks, this will likely improve overall
scheduling performance.

in one file, there are some parts of the system that make it sometimes less performant, or introduce more
delays than having those Dags split among many files. Just the fact that one file can only be parsed by one
FileProcessor, makes it less scalable for example. If you have many Dags generated from one file,
consider splitting them if you observe it takes a long time to reflect changes in your Dag files in the

Handling conflicting/complex Python dependencies

Airflow has many Python dependencies and sometimes the Airflow dependencies are conflicting with dependencies that your
task code expects. Since - by default - Airflow environment is just a single set of Python dependencies and single
Python environment, often there might also be cases that some of your tasks require different dependencies than other tasks
and the dependencies basically conflict between those tasks.

If you are using pre-defined Airflow Operators to talk to external services, there is not much choice, but usually those
operators will have dependencies that are not conflicting with basic Airflow dependencies. Airflow uses constraints mechanism
which means that you have a “fixed” set of dependencies that the community guarantees that Airflow can be installed with
(including all community providers) without triggering conflicts. However, you can upgrade the providers
independently and their constraints do not limit you, so the chance of a conflicting dependency is lower (you still have
to test those dependencies). Therefore, when you are using pre-defined operators, chance is that you will have
little, to no problems with conflicting dependencies.

your operators are written using custom python code, or when you want to write your own Custom Operator,
you might get to the point where the dependencies required by the custom code of yours are conflicting with those

your task will stop working because someone released a new version of a dependency or you might fall

that running tasks will still interfere with each other - for example subsequent tasks executed on the
same worker might be affected by previous tasks creating/modifying files etc.

The benefits of using those operators are:

You can run tasks with different sets of both Python and system level dependencies, or even tasks
written in completely different language or even different processor architecture (x86 vs. arm).

The environment used to run the tasks enjoys the optimizations and immutability of containers, where a
similar set of dependencies can effectively reuse a number of cached layers of the image, so the
environment is optimized for the case where you have multiple similar, but different environments.

The dependencies can be pre-vetted by the admins and your security team, no unexpected, new code will
be added dynamically. This is good for both, security and stability.

Strong process-level isolation between tasks. Tasks run in separate containers/pods and cannot
influence one another at the process or filesystem level. They can still interact through standard
Airflow mechanisms (XComs, connections, variables) via the Execution API. See

Airflow Security Model
for the full isolation model.

The drawbacks:

There is an overhead to start the tasks. Usually not as big as when creating virtual environments dynamically,
but still significant (especially for the
KubernetesPodOperator
).

In case of TaskFlow decorators, the whole method to call needs to be serialized and sent over to the
Docker Container or Kubernetes Pod, and there are system-level limitations on how big the method can be.
Serializing, sending, and finally deserializing the method on remote end also adds an overhead.

There is a resources overhead coming from multiple processes needed. Running tasks in case of those
two operators requires at least two processes - one process (running in Docker Container or Kubernetes Pod)
executing the task, and a supervising process in the Airflow worker that submits the job to
Docker/Kubernetes and monitors the execution.

Your environment needs to have the container images ready upfront. This usually means that you
cannot change them on the fly. Adding system dependencies, modifying or changing Python requirements
requires an image rebuilding and publishing (usually in your private registry).
Iteration time when you work on new dependencies are usually longer and require the developer who is

use and the top-level Python code of your Dag should not import/use those libraries.

You need to understand more details about how Docker Containers or Kubernetes work. The abstraction
provided by those two are “leaky”, so you need to understand a bit more about resources, networking,
containers etc. in order to author a Dag that uses those operators.

There is a possibility (though it requires a deep knowledge of Airflow deployment) to run Airflow tasks
using multiple, independent Docker images. This can be achieved via allocating different tasks to different

(at least currently) requires a lot of manual deployment configuration and intrinsic knowledge of how
Airflow, Celery and Kubernetes works. Also it introduces quite some overhead for running the tasks - there
are less chances for resource reuse and it’s much more difficult to fine-tune such a deployment for
cost of resources without impacting the performance and stability.

One of the possible ways to make it more useful is

spark.catalog.cacheTable("tableName")
or

.

This article describes best practices when using
Delta Lake
.

Best practices overview
​

The following are general recommendations that apply to most
Delta Lake
workloads:

Use
Unity Catalog
managed tables. See
Unity Catalog
managed tables for
Delta Lake
and
Apache Iceberg
.

Use predictive optimization. See
Predictive optimization for
Unity Catalog
managed tables
.

Use liquid clustering. See
Use liquid clustering for tables
.

When deleting and recreating a table in the same location, you should always use a
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE
statement. See
Drop or replace a table
.

Remove legacy Delta configurations
​

Databricks recommends removing most explicit legacy Delta configurations from Spark configurations and table properties when upgrading to a new
Databricks Runtime
version. Legacy configurations can prevent new optimizations and default values introduced by Databricks from being applied to migrated workloads.

Compact files
​

Predictive optimization automatically runs
OPTIMIZE
and
VACUUM
commands on
Unity Catalog
managed tables. See
Predictive optimization for
Unity Catalog
managed tables
.

Databricks recommends frequently running the
OPTIMIZE
command to compact small files.

note
This operation does not remove the old files. To remove them, run the
VACUUM
command.

Do not use Spark caching with
Delta Lake
​

Databricks does not recommend that you use Spark caching for the following reasons:

You lose any data skipping that can come from additional filters added on top of the cached
DataFrame
.

The data that gets cached might not be updated if the table is accessed using a different identifier.

Differences between
Delta Lake
and Parquet on
Apache Spark
​

Delta Lake
handles the following operations automatically. You should never perform these operations manually:

REFRESH TABLE
:
Delta Lake
tables always return the most up-to-date information, so there is no need to call
REFRESH TABLE
manually after changes.

Delta Lake
handles the following operations automatically. You should never perform these operations manually:

REFRESH TABLE
:
Delta Lake
tables always return the most up-to-date information, so there is no need to call
REFRESH TABLE
manually after changes.

Add and remove partitions
:
Delta Lake
automatically tracks the set of partitions present in a table and updates the list as data is added or removed. As a result, there is no need to run
ALTER TABLE [ADD|DROP] PARTITION
or
MSCK
.

Load a single partition
: Reading partitions directly is not necessary. For example, you don't need to run
spark.read.format("parquet").load("/data/date=2017-01-01")
. Instead, use a
WHERE
clause for data skipping, such as
spark.read.table("<table-name>").where("date = '2017-01-01'")
.

Don't manually modify data files
:
Delta Lake
uses the transaction log to commit changes to the table atomically. Do not directly modify, add, or delete Parquet data files in a
Delta Lake
table, because this can lead to lost data or table corruption.

Improve performance for
Delta Lake
merge
​

You can reduce the time it takes to merge by using the following approaches:

Reduce the search space for matches
: By default, the
merge
operation searches the entire
Delta Lake
table to find matches in the source table. One way to speed up
merge
is to reduce the search space by adding known constraints in the match condition. For example, suppose you have a table that is partitioned by
country
and
date
and you want to use
merge
to update information for the last day and a specific country. Adding the following condition makes the query faster, as it looks for matches only in the relevant partitions:

SQL
events
.
date

=

current_date
(
)

AND
events
.
country
=

'USA'

Furthermore, this query also reduces the chances of conflicts with other concurrent operations. See
Isolation levels and write conflicts
for more details.
